results.title: Contamination Percolation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Measurement Framework and Benchmark
results.abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are being deployed in healthcare, finance, and legal settings, yet we lack reliable methods for measuring how misinformation spreads through these networks. We introduce ContamPerc, a benchmark of 400 vignettes across 10 domains (8 clinical, 2 non-clinical), 50 domain-specific semantic markers, and a measurement pipeline that separates genuine contamination from defensive citations. The benchmark defines the Contamination Gap Diagnostic (CGD): a single number classifying a model's alignment behavior, computed from approximately 25,000 API calls via the released evaluation harness. We validate the framework with approximately 210,000 API calls across five production model families-DBRX-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and GPT-4o-mini-all at 100 trials per configuration with bootstrap significance testing. The CGD reveals five distinct alignment profiles spanning +55 to −62. Sensitivity analysis across three temperatures and two prompt phrasings confirms the diagnostic is robust. Cross-domain validation with three models on legal and financial vignettes confirms generalization beyond healthcare. An ablation across five models shows contamination occurs at the individual agent level, with one model (GPT-4o-mini) exhibiting a novel social dilution effect where peer context reduces contamination by 24 percentage points.

results.title: Are LLM-Agent Prompt-Injection Benchmarks Still Valid? A Cross-Model and Cross-Benchmark Study
results.abstract: Abstract Indirect prompt injection is the leading security problem for tool-using LLM agents, and a growing number of benchmarks have been developed to measure the robustness of the agents and the effectiveness of defenses against it. This work highlights an essential question which is often ignored in the research community: Is it true that these benchmarks are still applicable for current models, and is the robustness demonstrated on one benchmark portable to another benchmark, another vendor, or to another defense strategy? Using a unified, faithful, and configurable harness, we evaluate the attack success rate (ASR) of 11 models from five different vendors (Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, Mistral, DeepSeek) on two single-shot benchmarks with different threat models - InjecAgent (tool hijacking) and a targeted BIPIA-email injection (benign content insertion) and on the agent benchmark AgentDojo for four vendors, together with the evaluation of defense on ten models. Our findings show three primary results. First, benchmark saturation is vendor-specific: InjecAgent achieves 0% ASR on the Claude family of models, while other vendors are still vulnerable to attacks at rates ranging from 16% to 76%, indicating that the benchmark is only solved for Anthropic models. Second, the two single-shot benchmarks give conflicting evaluations of the robustness of the same models (e.g., Claude Opus 5 scores 0% ASR on InjecAgent, yet 59% on BIPIA). They have negatively correlated robustness ranking (Kendall’s τ = −0.24, permutation p = 0.41, underpowered with 11 models) and five out of eleven models are rated secure on one benchmark but vulnerable on the other. Third, none of the examined prompt-based defenses works universally across models.

results.title: ChainBench: An LLM Benchmark for Cross-Chain Code Generation
results.abstract: AI agents are increasingly capable of repositoryscale software work, and smart-contract engineering is a particularly high-stakes setting where toolchains and tests enforce correctness. We introduce ChainBench, a benchmark for cross-chain smart contract translation and contract generation built from production repositories and their real verification suites. Each task provides a structured specification and containerized environment: systems implement missing functionality to pass the existing verification suite, and are scored by Pass@1 task success. ChainBench contains 42 tasks spanning EVM Solidity, NEAR Rust, Aptos Move, Sui Move, and Starknet Cairo. In a zero-shot evaluation of nine deployed modelagent systems, including both standardized sameharness runs and preferred-harness runs where available, the best achieves 88.1% success, while several open-weight systems reach 52%-60% with substantially longer solve times. Performance further varies by target chain and task type, with failures ranging from narrow behavioral mismatches (e.g., missing edge-case guards) to build and repository-compatibility issues.

results.title: Semantic Method Naming and LLM Agent Accuracy: A Controlled Benchmark of REST/CRUD versus Agentic API Design
results.abstract:
As large language models take on AI agent roles, the design of the APIs they invoke becomes a measurable variable in task success. We investigate whether semantically rich method names aligned with user intent (BOOK, FIND, QUERY) produce higher endpoint selection accuracy than conventional REST/CRUD verbs (POST /reservations, GET /restaurants/search).

We developed the Agentic API Test Lab, a controlled benchmark with 36 natural-language tasks evaluated against a catalog of 24 CRUD and 21 agentic endpoint pairs. We conducted 7,200 trials across four LLM families (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Grok-3, GPT-4o, Llama 3.2 3B) spanning 18 experimental conditions.

In mixed-paradigm conditions, agentic methods outperform CRUD by 10–29 percentage points across all three frontier models (aggregate z = 3.77, p < 0.001). The effect is entirely absent in Llama 3.2 (0 pp, p = 0.95), establishing a capability threshold near 3B parameters. A description-swap ablation reveals the mechanism: CRUD endpoints given agentic-style descriptions collapse 39–43 pp (p < 0.001), while agentic endpoints given CRUD descriptions decline only 1–15 pp. Confidence calibration error spikes to +60–67 pp under description mismatch, indicating severe overconfidence precisely when models are most wrong.

API method naming is a measurable engineering variable with direct accuracy and safety consequences at frontier scale. The mechanism is not documentation quality but the method name itself, which encodes intent with sufficient density to survive documentation noise.

results.title: SMAUG: Semantic-Enhanced Mobile App Usage Data Generation With LLM
From Feature Lists to Enforced Invariants: AgentGov-Bench, a Deployability Benchmark for Multi-Agent LLM Orchestration Platforms
results.abstract: Context: Multi-agent systems built on large language models now plan, call tools and execute code in production settings. Benchmarks measure what such agents can do, and separate efforts measure robustness to prompt injection, but no standard measures whether the orchestration platform that runs them is deployable: whether it terminates, behaves consistently, recovers from faults and enforces governance controls. Objective: We propose AgentGov-Bench, a benchmark that scores a deployed multi-agent platform on four separately reported axes (capability, reliability, governance and cost) and treats governance as eight behavioural invariants to be tested, not as features to be listed. Method: We define the invariants, a test procedure and pass criterion for each, a reliability protocol and a non-fungible deployability profile, and a reference architecture whose components map one-to-one to the invariants. As preliminary evidence we audited the official documentation of five widely used open-source frameworks against the invariants. Results: All five document bounded termination and human-in-the-loop approval as built-in features. None documents per-agent identity as a built-in feature; three offer it through an integration or hosted service. Built-in sandboxed code execution is documented by one framework. The documentation also records conditions under which controls fail open or do not cover all tool types. Conclusion: Feature availability does not establish enforcement. Deployability must be measured on the configured system with behavioural tests, which AgentGov-Bench specifies.

results.title: AppEval: A Unified Benchmark for LLM-Based Mobile Application Repair in ArkTS, Swift, and Kotlin
results.abstract: Repository-level LLM agents are typically evaluated on projects whose tests run on the build host. It remains unclear whether their repairs survive the mobile build-install-launch-test boundary, where a missing SDK, offline device, or pre-assertion crash can be mistaken for a program failure. We present AppEval, a benchmark and native-toolchain evaluation framework for mobile application repair across HarmonyOS/ArkTS, iOS/Swift, and Android/Kotlin. Each task separates a hidden behavior test from the reference production fix and is accepted only when the same installed-app target reaches an assertion failure on the defective revision and passes after the fix; infrastructure failures remain a distinct outcome. A common schema maps this contract to each platform's build system, runtime, and test runner. The audited Android partition contains 200 accepted instrumentation tasks from 24 independently buildable repositories. On these tasks, five agents achieve Pass@1 between 22.00% and 90.50%, a 68.50-percentage-point spread under the same dynamic oracle. These results show that mobile repair performance depends strongly on the evaluated agent while demonstrating why runtime-aware acceptance is necessary for meaningful comparison. The quantitative findings in this paper are Android-specific; audited iOS and HarmonyOS results are required before drawing cross-platform generalization conclusions.
